chunks: The second type: A man who gathered ignorance, placed among the ignorant of the nation, treacherous in the thickets of strife,
blind to what is in the knot of peace; those resembling him have named him a scholar, but he is not so.
He rose early to collect much, of which little is better than much,
until when he quenched his thirst from stagnant water and acquired more than what is useful, he sat among the people as a judge responsible for clarifying what was confusing to others.
If an ambiguous issue came to him, he prepared for it a shabby stuffing of his own opinion, then decided by it,
so he is in the entanglement of doubts like the weaving of the spider: he does not know if he was right or wrong.
If he was right, he feared that he might have erred, and if he erred, he hoped that he might have been right.
An ignorant man, wanderer in ignorances, companion of the blind, who did not bite into knowledge with a decisive tooth, scattering traditions as the wind scatters dry leaves.
ai.seo_question: What are the characteristics of a false scholar who dispenses justice without true knowledge?
ai.summary: Imam Ali critiques the 'false scholar' (al-'alim ghayr al-'alim) who relies on superficial accumulation of knowledge and subjective opinion (ra'y) rather than deep understanding, a warning particularly relevant to the era of political and judicial instability. This figure is depicted as a 'weaver of doubts' whose judgments are as fragile as a spider's web, reflecting the Shia scholarly concern with distinguishing true gnosis from mere rhetorical skill in legal dispensation. The passage underscores the danger of unqualified individuals assuming judicial roles, a theme central to the governance principles outlined in Nahj al-Balagha.

en.sayed-ali-raza: The other man is he who has picked up ignorance.
He moves among the ignorant, is senseless in the thick of mischief and is blind to the advantages of peace. Those resembling like men have named him scholar but he is not so.
He goes out early morning to collect things whose deficiency is better than plenty, till when he has quenched his thirst from polluted water and acquired meaningless things.
He sits among the people as a judge responsible for solving whatever is confusing to the others.
If an ambiguous problem is presented before him he manages shabby argument about it of his own accord and passes judgement on its basis.
In this way he is entangled in the confusion of doubts as in the spider’s web, not knowing whether he was right or wrong.
If he is right he fears lest he erred, while if he is wrong he hopes he is right.

He is ignorant, wandering astray in ignorance and riding on carriages aimlessly moving in darkness. He did not try to find reality of knowledge. He scatters the traditions as the wind scatters the dry leaves.
